scenario: AITA for keeping my son during my visitation instead of giving in to his mother? | I guess some backstory is due here. My ex and I have an 8 year old son, and we have been split up for a few years now. I have every other weekend parenting time along with a day during the week. It’s not enough time for me, but it’s what was legally decided through court. Her and I do not have the best relationship currently because I feel like I’m always being taken advantage of and I allow it because she always uses the “it’s for your son” excuse. I cherish my time with my son, but for the longest time, I allowed my ex to alter the parenting schedule to suit my son’s needs, whether for activities or family or if he just wasn’t feeling well. I always tried to be as accommodating as possible, even if it meant I didn’t see him for a week or more. Anyway, last Wednesday I was supposed to get him overnight, his mother called me and I asked if he could stay there since his cousin from out of town was staying with them. I reluctantly agreed but told her I wanted to get him Thursday instead. She agreed, and when Thursday came around, I texted her after work and said I was on my way to get him. She said they weren’t home, and I had to press her for information why. She decided to take the kids to a lake and said I needed to stop being grumpy because my son was having fun. We argued back and forth and since I did not drive all the way out to the lake to get him when I shouldn’t have had to in the first place, I told her that we should switch weekends (last weekend was hers, this one is mine) so that I had my make up time and his activities with her that fell on my weekend wouldn’t be interrupted. She refused, so now that my weekend is coming up, I’m not getting him at my regular time today because he’s at an amusement park with her family, and I am expected to give up even more of my valuable time tomorrow for their annual 4th of July party. Am I the asshole for putting my foot down and keeping my son during their family function so that I can enjoy time my son during my scheduled time?

message.reasoning:
Okay, let's try to figure this out. The user is asking if they're the asshole for keeping their son during their visitation time instead of giving in to their ex's plans. 

First, I need to understand the scenario. The ex and the user have a legal custody arrangement where the user gets every other weekend plus a weekday. The user feels they're being taken advantage of, and the ex uses the "for the son's sake" excuse. The user has been accommodating, even adjusting their schedule when needed. 

Last week, the user was supposed to get their son overnight, but the ex changed the plans. The user wanted to pick up Thursday, but the ex took the kids to a lake. They argued, and the user decided to switch weekends to get make-up time. The ex refused, so now the user isn't getting their son at the regular time because he's at an amusement park with the ex's family, and the user has to give up more time for the 4th of July party.

The question is whether the user is being morally acceptable by keeping their son during their scheduled time instead of giving in. 

So, the key points here are the legal custody arrangement, the user's feelings of being taken advantage of, the ex's use of the child as an excuse, and the user's decision to enforce their visitation time. 

Morally, the user has a right to their scheduled visitation time as per the court order. The ex is using the child's time for their own family events, which might be against the agreed-upon schedule. The user's action of keeping the child during their scheduled time is about asserting their legal rights and ensuring the child gets the time they're entitled to. 

However, there's also the aspect of the child's well-being. If the ex is prioritizing their family events over the user's scheduled time, it might be affecting the child's relationship with both parents. The user's decision could be seen as standing up for their rights, which is morally acceptable. 

But the user's previous accommodation might have led to the ex taking advantage, so the user's current action is a form of setting boundaries. The ex's refusal to comply might be the issue, not the user's action. 

So, the user isn't the asshole here. They're trying to enforce their legal rights and ensure their time with the child isn't being undermined. The ex's actions are the problem, not the user's decision to keep the child during their scheduled time.
